Excluded were students who had signed the loyalty declaration in 1943 that was demanded of students in occupied Netherlands at the time (an exception was possible for students who had signed but had not continued their studies).[3]

value.text:
Temporary Academy was a temporary institution of higher education in Eindhoven, in the southern Netherlands, at the end of the Second World War. It was founded at the beginning of 1945, after Allied forces had liberated the south of the country in late 1944. The Temporary Academy foundation in Eindhoven was formally established on 26 February 1945 with approval from the Dutch government in exile. Balthasar van der Pol served as chairman, and Hendrik Casimir was rector.

The academy was intended, among other purposes, to train academics for the Philips Physics Laboratory. Universities and colleges offering programs in the exact sciences and engineering sciences were then situated in the still occupied north of the Netherlands. Students who had signed the loyalty declaration demanded in 1943 were excluded, although an exception was possible for signatories who had subsequently discontinued their studies. The academy continued operating after the liberation of the entire Netherlands in May 1945. By December that year, the other universities had resumed their regular programs, removing the need for the temporary institution, and it closed. A university institution returned to Eindhoven in 1956 with the establishment of Eindhoven University of Technology.
